Generalized policy iteration: judge, improve, repeat

The loop of evaluation and improvement inside most reinforcement learning methods, worked through on the cliff grid and traced from dynamic programming to AlphaGo Zero.

October 23, 20269 min read

reinforcement-learningmachine-learning

Take Part 1's 4 by 12 cliff grid: start S bottom left, flag G bottom right, ten cliff cells between. Each move gives −1, the cliff gives −100 and sends you back to S, walls keep you in place, and the discount is γ=0.99\gamma = 0.99γ=0.99. If you know these rules, can you just work out the best way to move?

Trying all 437≈1.9×10224^{37} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{22}437≈1.9×1022 rules, one move in each of 37 cells, is hopeless. To improve a rule you must score it first, and each new rule needs a new score.

This side article to my reinforcement learning series follows Chapter 4 of Sutton and Barto (page numbers refer to its second edition).

How good is the current rule?

Start with a random walker that picks each move with chance ¼. Such a rule is a policy π\piπ, with π(a∣s)\pi(a \mid s)π(a∣s) the chance it picks move aaa in cell sss. The value vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) is the total discounted reward you collect on average from sss under π\piπ. Computing it is policy evaluation (§4.1, p. 74), and each value depends on the cells one move can reach (eq. 4.4, p. 74):

vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vπ(s′)]v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big] vπ​(s)=a∑​π(a∣s)s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ​(s′)]

The model p(s′,r∣s,a)p(s', r \mid s, a)p(s′,r∣s,a) is the chance that move aaa in sss lands in s′s's′ with reward rrr. You know it, so that's 37 linear equations in 37 unknowns. You can solve them directly, or in sweeps: replace every value with the right-hand side, using the current guesses, and repeat until the values barely move. Panel 1 shows the solution: about −482 above the flag, −1072 at S.

Solving for the values

My script (linked under "Every round") solves the equations directly. Written out, a sweep is (eq. 4.5, p. 74):

vk+1(s)=∑aπ(a∣s)∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γ vk(s′)]\begin{aligned} v_{k+1}(s) &= \sum_a \pi(a \mid s) \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a) \\ &\qquad \big[r + \gamma\, v_k(s')\big] \end{aligned} vk+1​(s)​=a∑​π(a∣s)s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvk​(s′)]​

For γ<1\gamma < 1γ<1, repeated sweeps converge to vπv_\pivπ​ in the limit, from any start with the flag at 0 (pp. 74-75).

Act greedily on those numbers

The action value is what you get from making move aaa once, then following π\piπ (eq. 4.6, p. 78):

qπ(s,a)=∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vπ(s′)]q_\pi(s, a) = \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\big] qπ​(s,a)=s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ​(s′)]

The greedy policy takes the best move in each cell (eq. 4.9, p. 79):

π′(s)=arg⁡max⁡aqπ(s,a)\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a q_\pi(s, a) π′(s)=argamax​qπ​(s,a)

Here π′(s)\pi'(s)π′(s) is a single move, and switching to it is policy improvement. One greedy step (panel 2) funnels the ten red cells of the left three columns into the top-left corner, which the walker rated above both its neighbors. There they bump the top wall forever: −1 per step, or −1/(1−γ)=−100-1/(1-\gamma) = -100−1/(1−γ)=−100 in total. S never reaches the flag now, yet its value went from −1072 to −100, and all 37 cells improved.

By the policy improvement theorem (eq. 4.7 and 4.8, p. 78), if taking the new move once and then following π\piπ is never worse than following π\piπ from the start,

qπ(s,π′(s))≥vπ(s)for every s,q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \ge v_\pi(s) \quad \text{for every } s, qπ​(s,π′(s))≥vπ​(s)for every s,

then vπ′(s)≥vπ(s)v_{\pi'}(s) \ge v_\pi(s)vπ′​(s)≥vπ​(s) everywhere. So use the new move again at the next step, and the next. After kkk steps, all that's left of the old policy is its value kkk steps ahead, discounted by γk\gamma^kγk, which shrinks to zero. Greedy always meets the condition: vπ(s)=∑aπ(a∣s) qπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, q_\pi(s, a)vπ​(s)=∑a​π(a∣s)qπ​(s,a) is an average of action values, and the max is at least the average.

The proof chain (p. 78)

Unroll the condition step by step:

vπ(s)≤qπ(s,π′(s))=E[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s,At=π′(s)]=Eπ′[Rt+1+γvπ(St+1)∣St=s]≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γqπ(St+1,π′(St+1))∣St=s]=Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2vπ(St+2)∣St=s]≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+γ3vπ(St+3)∣St=s]    ⋮≤Eπ′[Rt+1+γRt+2+γ2Rt+3+γ3Rt+4+⋯∣St=s]=vπ′(s)\begin{aligned} v_\pi(s) &\le q_\pi(s, \pi'(s)) \\ &= \mathbb{E}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s, A_t = \pi'(s)\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma q_\pi(S_{t+1}, \pi'(S_{t+1})) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 v_\pi(S_{t+2}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \gamma^3 v_\pi(S_{t+3}) \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &\;\;\vdots \\ &\le \mathbb{E}_{\pi'}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \gamma^3 R_{t+4} + \cdots \mid S_t = s\big] \\ &= v_{\pi'}(s) \end{aligned} vπ​(s)​≤qπ​(s,π′(s))=E[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s,At​=π′(s)]=Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γvπ​(St+1​)∣St​=s]≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γqπ​(St+1​,π′(St+1​))∣St​=s]=Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2vπ​(St+2​)∣St​=s]≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+γ3vπ​(St+3​)∣St​=s]⋮≤Eπ′​[Rt+1​+γRt+2​+γ2Rt+3​+γ3Rt+4​+⋯∣St​=s]=vπ′​(s)​

Here Eπ′\mathbb{E}_{\pi'}Eπ′​ averages over following π′\pi'π′, and each ≤\le≤ uses the condition at the next cell. The theorem also covers stochastic policies like the random walker (p. 79).

Repeat until nothing changes

The values now belong to the old policy, so you evaluate again and improve again. That's policy iteration (§4.3, p. 80), with E a full evaluation and I a greedy improvement:

π0→  E  vπ0→  I  π1→  E  vπ1→  I  π2→  E  ⋯→  I  π∗→  E  v∗\begin{aligned} &\pi_0 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_{\pi_0} \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_1 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_{\pi_1} \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_2 \\ &\xrightarrow{\;E\;} \cdots \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_* \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_* \end{aligned} ​π0​E​vπ0​​I​π1​E​vπ1​​I​π2​E​⋯I​π∗​E​v∗​​

It takes six rounds of one evaluation and one greedy step each (panel 3); panel 2 showed round 1. In rounds 2 to 4, the stuck red cells come free a column at a time. In round 4 S finds a 17-step route (−15.71), and in round 6 a 13-step route along the cliff edge (−12.25), the route and score Q-learning found in Part 1.

After round 6 a greedy step changes nothing, so the loop stops. No change means every value already equals its best action value: vπ(s)=max⁡aqπ(s,a)v_\pi(s) = \max_a q_\pi(s, a)vπ​(s)=maxa​qπ​(s,a) in every cell. That's the Bellman optimality equation (eq. 4.1, p. 73), and in a finite problem its only solution is v∗v_*v∗​, the best value any policy can reach. So the final policy is optimal (pp. 64 and 79). It must stop, too: with the tie rule in the drawer, each change makes some cell strictly better, so no policy comes back, and only finitely many policies pick one move per cell.

Why it stops, written out

When two moves tie, the policy keeps its current move (the fix that Exercise 4.4 asks for, p. 82), so a round only switches to strictly better moves. Then some cell gets strictly better (p. 78), so no policy can come back. With finitely many deterministic policies, the ones that pick one move per cell, the loop must stop (p. 80).

At the stop π′=π\pi' = \piπ′=π, and written out with the model, its values satisfy (eq. 4.1, p. 73)

vπ′(s)=max⁡a∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vπ′(s′)]v_{\pi'}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_{\pi'}(s')\big] vπ′​(s)=amax​s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvπ′​(s′)]

Two processes, any amount of work

Policy iteration runs evaluation to the end before each greedy step. It doesn't have to. Value iteration stops evaluation after one sweep and does the greedy step inside it: a max over moves replaces the average over π\piπ's moves (eq. 4.10, p. 83):

vk+1(s)=max⁡a∑s′,rp(s′,r∣s,a) [r+γ vk(s′)]v_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_k(s')\big] vk+1​(s)=amax​s′,r∑​p(s′,r∣s,a)[r+γvk​(s′)]

On the cliff grid, from all zeros, it reaches v∗v_*v∗​ exactly at sweep 14, though in general it only converges in the limit (p. 83).

The general idea is generalized policy iteration (GPI): "letting policy-evaluation and policy-improvement processes interact, independent of the granularity and other details of the two processes" (§4.6, p. 86). In panel 4, evaluation pulls V, the current value estimate, toward vπv_\pivπ​, and improvement pulls π\piπ toward greedy(V). If both stop changing, V is the policy's true value and the policy is fully greedy for it, the stop condition from above, so you're at an optimal π∗\pi_*π∗​ and v∗v_*v∗​ (p. 86). And "Almost all reinforcement learning methods are well described as GPI" (p. 86).

Two goals that pull apart

In panel 5, the book's sketch (p. 87), each point pairs a value table vvv with a policy π\piπ. The blue line is v=vπv = v_\piv=vπ​, where the values fit the policy, and the green line is π=greedy(v)\pi = \text{greedy}(v)π=greedy(v). Each jump onto one line usually knocks you off the other: new values can favor new moves, and a new policy makes old values wrong. Yet the zigzag climbs to where they meet, the optimum, for the reasons in section 3. The two processes "can be viewed as both competing and cooperating" (p. 86).

The same loop inside other methods

Without the model, most methods run both processes on experience (panel 6).

  • Monte Carlo control (§5.2-5.3, pp. 96-99) evaluates by averaging what whole episodes earn. Without a model, vvv can't pick a move (p. 96), so it learns action values Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) and acts greedily on them after each episode. In the book's version, Monte Carlo with exploring starts (ES), episodes start from a random cell and move, so every move gets tried (pp. 98-99).
  • Sarsa (§6.4, p. 129) nudges Q(s,a)Q(s,a)Q(s,a) toward one reward plus the next estimate, a temporal-difference (TD) update, and acts ε-greedy (mostly greedy, sometimes random). That's "the pattern of generalized policy iteration (GPI), only this time using TD methods for the evaluation or prediction part".
  • Q-learning (§6.5, p. 131) puts the max inside its TD target, R+γmax⁡aQ(S′,a)R + \gamma \max_a Q(S', a)R+γmaxa​Q(S′,a), so improvement happens inside every evaluation update (Figure 8.6, p. 172).
  • Actor-critic (§13.5, p. 331): the actor is a policy updated by gradient steps. The critic evaluates the actor's policy with TD and the actor improves it (p. 346), though the book never names this GPI outright (see Sources).
  • AlphaGo Zero, the book says, "implemented a form of policy iteration (Section 4.3), interleaving policy evaluation with policy improvement" (§16.6.2, p. 447).

Silver et al. (2017) agree. A network outputs move probabilities ppp and a value vvv (the paper's symbols). Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) guided by it returns search probabilities π\piπ that usually select much stronger moves than ppp: "MCTS may therefore be viewed as a powerful policy improvement operator". Self-play with search "may be viewed as a powerful policy evaluation operator". Training moves vvv toward the game winner zzz (evaluation) and ppp toward π\piπ (improvement), and the paper uses these operators "repeatedly in a policy iteration procedure".

AlphaGo Zero's loss

The network fθf_\thetafθ​ maps a board sss to (p,v)=fθ(s)(p, v) = f_\theta(s)(p,v)=fθ​(s). Training adjusts θ\thetaθ to minimize (eq. 1, p. 6)

l=(z−v)2−π⊤log⁡p+c ∥θ∥2l = (z - v)^2 - \pi^\top \log p + c\,\lVert\theta\rVert^2 l=(z−v)2−π⊤logp+c∥θ∥2

  • (z−v)2(z - v)^2(z−v)2 is evaluation: vvv moves toward the winner zzz, +1+1+1 or −1-1−1 from the current player's side.
  • −π⊤log⁡p-\pi^\top \log p−π⊤logp is improvement: ppp moves toward the search probabilities π\piπ.
  • c ∥θ∥2c\,\lVert\theta\rVert^2c∥θ∥2 is weight regularization.

What I take from it

Now, in any new method, I look for the two processes. What judges the policy? What turns that judgment into a better policy? And how far does each go before handing over? Most methods in the series differ in those three answers.

Sources
  • Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed., 2018. Q-learning's GPI label comes from Chapter 6 (pp. 119 and 138), not §6.5. No page says that actor-critic is a form of GPI: p. 138 calls it "a third way in which TD methods can be extended to control", but p. 460 lists them as separate ways to learn a policy.
  • Silver et al., Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge, Nature, 2017. Pages refer to the author version, and the quotes are on p. 3.
  • Haarnoja et al., Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor, ICML 2018. More direct than the book: "Actor-critic algorithms are typically derived starting from policy iteration" (p. 2 of the arXiv version).
